name: Omeprazole
mechanism: Irreversibly inhibits gastric H+/K+-ATPase (proton pump) in parietal cells, blocking final step of acid secretion. Prodrug activated in acidic environment of parietal cell canaliculi. Profound acid suppression (>90% ↓ 24h acid output). Duration of action exceeds half-life (pump regeneration required for acid secretion recovery - takes 2-3 days)
dosing: GORD: 20mg OD for 4-8 weeks (maintenance 10-20mg OD if needed). Peptic ulcer (gastric/duodenal): 20-40mg OD for 4-8 weeks. H. pylori eradication: 20-40mg BD with antibiotics for 7-14 days. NSAID-associated ulcer prophylaxis: 20mg OD. Zollinger-Ellison: 60mg OD, titrate up (120-160mg/day in divided doses). Take 30-60 min before food (requires food-stimulated acid secretion for activation). Swallow whole (enteric-coated). IV if oral not possible (40-80mg daily)
contraindications: Hypersensitivity to PPIs or substituted benzimidazoles. Concurrent with nelfinavir (PPI ↓ nelfinavir levels). Caution: osteoporosis (long-term PPI ↑ fracture risk), hypomagnesaemia, C. difficile risk, severe hepatic impairment (reduce dose)
interactions: Clopidogrel: omeprazole inhibits CYP2C19 (prodrug activation) → ↓ antiplatelet effect (↑ CV events). AVOID - use lansoprazole/pantoprazole if PPI needed. Warfarin: may ↑ INR (monitor). CYP2C19 substrate interactions: diazepam, phenytoin (↑ levels). ↓ Absorption of pH-dependent drugs: ketoconazole, itraconazole, erlotinib, dasatinib (requires gastric acid). ↑ Digoxin levels (monitor). Methotrexate: ↑ levels (high-dose MTX - toxicity risk). St John's Wort ↓ omeprazole levels
monitoring: Symptom control (dyspepsia, reflux). Review need regularly - aim for lowest effective dose, shortest duration. Long-term use (>1 year): vitamin B12 (annual - malabsorption), magnesium (annually if risk factors: diuretics, digoxin), bone density (if osteoporosis risk). Consider H. pylori testing/eradication if recurrent ulcers. Endoscopy if alarm symptoms (dysphagia, weight loss, anaemia, persistent vomiting). CYP2C19 polymorphisms affect efficacy (poor metabolizers ↑ exposure, extensive/ultra-rapid ↓ exposure)
pregnancy: Generally considered safe - extensive human data, no increased malformation risk. Use if needed. First choice PPI in pregnancy (most data). Benefits usually outweigh risks for severe reflux/ulcers
sideEffects: Common: headache, GI upset (nausea, diarrhoea, constipation, abdominal pain), dizziness. Long-term/high-dose: hypomagnesaemia (muscle cramps, arrhythmias, seizures - check Mg if symptoms), vitamin B12 deficiency (achlorhydria ↓ absorption), ↑ fracture risk (hip, wrist, spine - impaired Ca absorption), microscopic colitis, C. difficile infection (↑ risk - loss of gastric acid barrier), community-acquired pneumonia (↑ risk), acute interstitial nephritis (rare - AKI), SLE exacerbation (rare). Rare: hyponatraemia, hepatotoxicity, blood dyscrasias, Stevens-Johnson syndrome
pharmacokinetics: Prodrug activated in acidic environment of parietal cells. Well absorbed (enteric-coated to prevent premature acid degradation). Bioavailability ~35-65% (increases with repeated dosing - less acid to degrade). Peak 1-2h. Protein-bound (95%). Extensively metabolized by CYP2C19 (major) and CYP3A4 (minor). Half-life: 0.5-1h (but duration of action 24-72h due to irreversible pump binding). Excreted in urine (80% metabolites). CYP2C19 polymorphisms: poor metabolizers (↑ levels, greater acid suppression), ultra-rapid metabolizers (↓ levels, may need higher doses)
clinicalPearls: First PPI (1989). Generic, inexpensive, widely used. GORD: effective for symptom control and healing erosive oesophagitis. Start 20mg OD, increase to 40mg if inadequate response. Maintenance therapy often needed (Barrett's, severe oesophagitis). Non-erosive reflux: trial 4-8 weeks, then stop if improved (lifestyle measures). PEPTIC ULCER: equally effective as other PPIs for healing. H. pylori eradication critical (prevents recurrence). Test (urea breath test, stool antigen, endoscopy biopsy) and treat if positive (triple therapy: PPI BD + clarithromycin + amoxicillin for 7-14 days). NSAID ULCER PROPHYLAXIS: PPI first-line in high-risk (age >65, previous ulcer/bleed, concurrent steroids/anticoagulants/SSRIs). More effective and better tolerated than misoprostol. CLOPIDOGREL INTERACTION: AVOID omeprazole/esomeprazole (CYP2C19 inhibition ↓ clopidogrel activation). Use lansoprazole or pantoprazole if PPI needed post-ACS. FDA warning 2009. LONG-TERM RISKS: hypomagnesaemia (monitor if diuretics/digoxin), B12 deficiency (annual check if >1 year use), fractures (ensure adequate Ca/vitamin D, bisphosphonates if osteoporosis), C. diff/pneumonia (↑ infection risk). DEPRESCRIBING: review regularly. Many on PPIs long-term without clear indication. Attempt step-down (reduce to 10mg or alternate days) or STOP (trial off, use on-demand for symptoms). Rebound hypersecretion common 2 weeks after stopping (transient). ALTERNATIVES: H2RAs (ranitidine - now withdrawn, famotidine) less effective but fewer long-term concerns. Antacids/alginates for mild symptoms. Fundoplication surgery for refractory GORD. ADMINISTRATION: take 30-60 min before breakfast (requires food-stimulated acid secretion for optimal activation, but paradoxically give before food). Swallow whole - capsule can be opened and granules sprinkled on food if swallowing difficulty (don't chew). IV for acute upper GI bleeding (80mg bolus, then 8mg/h infusion) - reduces rebleeding risk post-endoscopy. OTC: 10-20mg available for short-term GORD (max 4 weeks, then seek medical advice). Most widely used PPI globally. Cost-effective
indication: Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GORD), peptic ulcer disease (gastric and duodenal), H. pylori eradication (combination therapy), NSAID-associated ulcer treatment/prophylaxis, Zollinger-Ellison syndrome (gastrinoma), dyspepsia, upper GI bleeding (IV)
